title: Indra Stays 101 Years
hookLine: a god and a demon go to learn the self; the demon leaves happy with the wrong answer, and Indra keeps coming back
carry: moksha: freedom from the round of birth and death
tomorrow: Arjuna asks to see Krishna as he really is. why does he need new eyes?

lines: A SELF BEYOND DEATH AND GRIEF.
cards: Near the end of the Chandogya Upanishad, Prajapati, the creator, announces: there is a self free from old age, death, grief, hunger and thirst. Whoever finds it gains everything. The gods send Indra.
The asuras send their king, Virochana. They live as students for thirty-two years. Then Prajapati tells them: look at yourselves in a pan of water, dressed in your best.
That's the self. Virochana goes home delighted. The body is the self!
And that's what he teaches. Indra gets halfway home and stops. Wait.

teach.b: So Indra goes back. Thirty-two more years. Prajapati says: the self is the one who roams in dreams.
Indra thinks it over: but in dreams you can still suffer. Back again, thirty-two more years. The self is the one in deep sleep.

But then you know nothing at all. Back once more, five more years, a hundred and one in all. And Prajapati finally says: this body is mortal, held by death, but it's the home of the self that doesn't die.
That's the teaching: atman, the self, isn't the body, and knowing it frees you. Hindus call that freedom moksha, release from samsara, the round of birth, death and rebirth.
The Chandogya ends with the one who reaches Brahman: he does not return, he does not return.
And the Brahma Sutra, which opened with now, the wish to know, closes the same way: no return, said twice. The schools fill in what freedom is.

For Shankara, it's knowing what was always so: the self was never anything but Brahman. For Ramanuja and Madhva, the freed self stays itself and lives with the Lord, whom they know as Vishnu, in a joy that doesn't end.
So when an elder says she prays not to come back, she isn't asking for less life.
She's asking for freedom. Like Indra, she just wants the real answer.

how: Hindus speak of moksha, release from samsara, as life's highest aim, and many elders pray for it; traditional students read the Brahma Sutra from its first line to its last, 'no return', said twice, usually through their own lineage's commentary.

o: a rite that closes each year by ringing a second bell
a heaven where the body lives forever unchanged
freedom from the round of birth, death and rebirth

p: goes home sure the body is the self

s: in the Chandogya, Prajapati's first answer satisfies Indra
Indra sees the body grows old and dies, and goes back three more times.
no return means the same thing in every Vedanta school
Shankara: knowing the self was always Brahman; Ramanuja and Madhva: life with the Lord in joy.
praying not to come back is a prayer for moksha, freedom
it asks for release from the round of birth and death, not for less life.

games.q: Prajapati says the self is the one who dreams. Indra notices dreamers still suffer. what does he do?
o: accept it and go home, like Virochana
decide there is no self at all
games.why: he goes back, 101 years in all, until he hears of the deathless self. that's the seeker's way in Vedanta.

practice: Sit and notice your body, the weight, the warmth. That's known. Then notice your thoughts passing, like a dream.
That's known too. Then ask gently, like Indra: who is knowing all this? Don't answer.
Rest in the knowing for a few breaths. If you pray, you can rest in the presence of the One you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Vedanta. From the first word, now, the wish to know, to the last, no return, said twice: freedom. Today's word, and the last of our visit with it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: release, freedom; the highest aim of life in Hindu teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: moksha, freedom from the round of birth and death. Like Indra, don't stop at the first answer. Rest well.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7-8.12 (Prajapati's teaching; Indra and Virochana; the reflection, the dreamer, deep sleep; 101 years; the mortal body as the home of the deathless self)
Chandogya Upanishad 8.15.1 (he does not return, he does not return)
Brahma Sutra 4.4.22 (no return, on the authority of scripture; repeated)
Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva on Brahma Sutra 4.4 (the state of the freed self)
